title: Fencing Two Colours
statement: In the plane there are $2013$ red points and $2014$ blue points, and no three of these $4027$ points are collinear. Some lines are drawn, none of them through any of the points, and they divide the plane into regions. Determine the least positive integer $k$ with the following property: for every such set of $4027$ points, one can draw $k$ lines so that no region contains points of both colours.
hints: For a lower bound, place as many points as possible around a circle with the colours alternating. For an upper bound, find a way to cut two points of the same colour off from all the others.

Two lines parallel to $XY$, one on each side and very close to it, cut the two points $X$ and $Y$ off from every other point. One line can cut off a vertex of the convex hull, or two neighbouring vertices of it.
Pair up points of one colour, using two lines per pair. Look at the colours of the vertices of the convex hull to save a line.
solution: The answer is $k = 2013$. Lower bound. Place $2013$ red and $2013$ blue points alternately on a circle, and the last blue point anywhere off the circle, with no three of the points collinear. Consecutive points on the circle have different colours, so each of the $4026$ chords joining consecutive points must be crossed by a line: a region is an intersection of half-planes, so it is convex, and a region containing both ends of a chord would contain the whole chord. These chords are the sides of a convex $4026$-gon, and a line through none of its vertices crosses at most two of its sides. So at least $2013$ lines are needed. Upper bound. Given two of the points, $X$ and $Y$, no other point lies on line $XY$. So two lines parallel to $XY$, one on each side of it and close enough, bound a strip containing $X$ and $Y$ and no other point. Every region that contains $X$ or $Y$ lies in the strip, so it contains no point other than $X$ and $Y$. In the same way, one line parallel to a side $XY$ of the convex hull, just inside it, cuts the two neighbouring hull vertices $X$ and $Y$ off from the rest, and one line can cut a single hull vertex off from the rest. If some vertex of the convex hull is red, cut it off with one line, and split the other $2012$ red points into $1006$ pairs, each cut off with two lines. If every vertex of the convex hull is blue, cut off two neighbouring hull vertices with one line, and split the other $2012$ blue points into $1006$ pairs, each cut off with two lines. Either way there are $1 + 2 \cdot 1006 = 2013$ lines. Every region containing a point of a group lies on that group's side of its lines, so it contains only points of that group, all of one colour; every other region contains only points of the other colour. Moving the lines slightly if needed, none passes through a point. $\blacksquare$

solution_figures.alt: The lower-bound construction drawn small: three red points, labelled R and drawn in the accent colour, and three blue points, labelled B, alternate around a circle, and one more blue point lies off the circle. Every chord joining neighbouring points on the circle joins two colours, so some line must cross it. The highlighted line crosses exactly two sides of the hexagon formed by the six points, and no line can cross more than two.

rubric.criterion: States the answer $2013$, with either a correct construction for the lower bound or a correct strategy for the upper bound. The answer alone earns nothing.

Proves that $2013$ lines may be needed, for example with $2013$ red and $2013$ blue points alternating on a circle: each chord between consecutive points must be crossed, and a line crosses at most two sides of a convex polygon. Deduct 1 if it is not justified that a region containing both ends of a chord contains the chord.
Shows that two lines can cut any two points of the set off from all the others, or an equivalent separating lemma.

Completes the upper bound with $2013$ lines, using the convex hull (one line for a red hull vertex, or for two neighbouring blue hull vertices) and pairs of one colour, and checks that every region is of one colour.

fatal_errors.error: The upper bound pairs points of different colours, or otherwise leaves a region that can contain both colours.
Proves only that $2014$ lines always suffice, with no saving from the convex hull.
The lower bound counts regions or lines in a way that does not apply to every arrangement of the lines.
